definition: An unsupervised learning technique that groups data points into clusters based on similarity, without predefined labels.
details: Common clustering algorithms include k-means and hierarchical clustering, used for tasks like customer segmentation, anomaly detection, and exploratory data analysis.

explainer.lead: Clustering finds natural groups in data without being told what those groups should be. It helps people explore unfamiliar datasets, spot unusual points, and organize similar items together.

tiers.eli5: Imagine emptying a box of mixed buttons onto a table and putting similar ones into piles. You might group them by size, color, or shape without knowing their names in advance. Clustering does something similar with data points.
tiers.practitioner: Clustering is applied to unlabeled data with methods such as k-means and hierarchical clustering. Typical uses include customer segmentation, anomaly detection, and exploratory data analysis. The resulting groups still need interpretation: similarity-based clusters are not automatically meaningful categories.
tiers.paperLevel: Given unlabeled points x1, ..., xn, clustering partitions them into groups C1, ..., Ck so that membership is based on similarity rather than predefined labels. Common algorithmic families include k-means and hierarchical clustering. The absence of labels means that the learned clusters do not come with predefined semantic names.

explainer.example: A business has customer records but no predefined customer types. It applies clustering to group similar customers, then inspects the resulting segments as part of customer segmentation.

usedIn.name: Customer segmentation
usedIn.detail: Groups customers by similarity to reveal segments within an unlabeled customer dataset.

usedIn.name: Anomaly detection
usedIn.detail: Helps identify unusual data points during analysis based on how they relate to discovered groups.

usedIn.name: Exploratory data analysis
usedIn.detail: Reveals possible group structure when exploring data without predefined categories.

explainer.intuition: Clustering is like sorting an unfamiliar collection into piles of similar items. The piles emerge from the data instead of following labels supplied beforehand.
howItWorks: Start with data points that have no predefined labels.
Compare points using a notion of similarity.
Apply an algorithm such as k-means or hierarchical clustering.
Assign or arrange points into clusters of similar items.
Examine the resulting groups to understand what they may represent.
explainer.whyItMatters: Clustering provides a way to discover structure when labeled examples are unavailable. It can turn an unorganized dataset into groups that support exploration, segmentation, and the search for unusual points.
misconceptions: Clustering is not classification: it does not learn from predefined labels.
A discovered cluster is not automatically a meaningful real-world category; its interpretation requires examination.

nodes.label: Clustering algorithm
nodes.note: For example, k-means or hierarchical clustering

diagram.caption: Clustering turns unlabeled points into similarity-based groups for further analysis.
